newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Afghan government calls on world to reject rebels.
newsitem.headline: Afghan government calls on world to reject rebels.

text.p: Afghanistan's government, ousted from the capital of Kabul by radical Islamic militia, on Friday called on the world not to recognise any regime the rebels would create.

Adbul Rahim Ghafoorzai, Afghanistan's deputy foreign minister, said President Burhanuddin Rabbani and his advisers had retreated to the north of Kabul to Parwan and Kapisa provinces and were contemplating their next move.
Ghafoorzai, in New York to attend the U.N. General Assembly session, blamed Pakistan for Taleban's success.
Pakistan's U.N. ambassador, Ahmad Kamal, said the old government was finished and that the Taleban was in complete control of Kabul.

Reading a statement issued by Rabbani, Ghafoorzai, said that "the Islamic State of Afghanistan declares that any administration to be announced by this group, dependent on the outside, will have no legal or Islamic law credibility and therefore, will be rejected by the Afghan nation."

Ghafoorzai said he wanted the U.N. Security Council, meeting for hours on the Middle East on Friday, to take a position and had written it a letter. Diplomats said Russia wanted a council statement to register the day's events.

The Taleban controls more than half the central Asian country, which has been the scene of continual fighting between various Moslem and ethnic groups since Soviet troops supporting a communist government withdrew in 1989.

Emerging from the obscurity of Sunni Moslem religious schools in Pakistan two years ago, the group has been fighting to oust Rabbani's coalition Moslem government and impose a strict Islamic order across Afghanistan.
In some of the first measures enforced on Friday, they barred women from offices until further orders and asked them to wear the traditional Islamic veil when outside their homes.
Pakistan's Kamal said the Taleban had "advanced into Kabul without any significant level of fighting." He said that their advance was "noticeable for defections and desertions of government troops."

Kamal contended that the Taleban militia's top leader, Mullah Mohammad Rabbani, had already named himself as head of the country's six-man Supreme Council, and appointed Mullah Mohammad Ghaus as his foreign minister.
He said that Burhanuddin Rabbani, the retreating president who has the same last name as the Taleban leader, had fled to the Tajikistan border.

His chief commander, Ahmad Shah Masood, had withdrawn some of his forces and aircraft to Kunduz, close to areas controlled by General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who is a foe of the ousted president Rabbani but despised by the Taleban for his Communist past, Kamal said.

Kamal said the ousted government had no legitimacy since it was put into office to organise elections in 1994 and did not do so, adding: "That is why the Taleban have been able to advance with the degree of popular support they have."
Ghafoorzai maintained the government still had the capability to mount a military attack but would not do so in the capital where too many civilian lives were at stake.

He said the government controlled Parwan Kapisa, Baghldad, Kunduz, Takhar and Badakhshan as well as parts of Kabul province, while General Dostum had six areas under his jurisdiction. Both he and Taleban leaders maintained they wanted to negotiate with Dostum.

He said that it was dangerous to allow the Taleban to govern alone, adding that their cruelty in executing and stringing up former President Najibullah whom they abducted from a U.N. compound showed what they were about.
"It should be understood that the Taleban, with their agenda, should not be left alone and unchecked," he said. "A strong force to check and balance the Taleban is needed."

Pakistan has denied charges from the Afghan government as well as foreign diplomats that it has supported Taleban to keep the country off balance. But it says that it has no favourites among the Afghan factions, most of which it helped in their guerrilla war against Soviet occupation in the 1980s.
